<reason>A tight, high-quality debate. PRO built a clean comparative frame—which lever reaches the household that does nothing—and kept it live to the end: deductions presuppose enrollment, action, and taxable income, and CON conceded "no deduction touches zero." PRO's asset-shifting argument (deductions mostly relabel existing wealth) was never squarely answered by CON. CON landed real hits: escalation lies outside the motion, cashing out at job change is a taxed emergency fund, and PRO's own admission that opt-outs skew toward stressed low earners complicates the rescue story. But CON's central relocation of the cliff to middle earners rested on the unsupported assertion that they "overwhelmingly already hold accounts," which sits awkwardly against PRO's uncontested participation-gap framing, and CON's attempt to strip out the employer match was neatly reversed by PRO's closing (an uncaptured match is worth nothing; enrollment unlocks it). CON's turn was also clipped and its closing largely recapped Rebuttal 2. PRO made the decision easier: even on CON's "balance, not box" metric, a balance must first exist, and only one policy creates it for non-actors.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The employer-match exchange: CON argued in [B4.4] that the match belongs to the plan and a voluntary enrollee captures it identically, so PRO's wealth arithmetic collapses to an anchored three percent. PRO's closing [A5.3] turned it—an unclaimed match is worth zero, and auto-enrollment is precisely what delivers it to the worker who never files paperwork—preserving PRO's answer to CON's "bare policy" pressure question.</best_rebuttal>
